We present 9 concrete instances illustrating the three primary failure modes: output degeneracy, LP confidence inversion, and consensus-based verification failure. All examples use Qwen3-8B on Few-NERD ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$) from the MF4v2 pipeline.

\paragraph{Degenerate instances (3/3).}
All $N$ samples produce identical entity sets, eliminating any room for selection or construction improvement.

\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item \textbf{Type confusion.} \textit{``His undergraduate studies at the University of Notre Dame were interrupted by Army service in World War II.''} Gold: \{University of Notre Dame / building\}. All 8 samples: \{University of Notre Dame / \textbf{organization}, World War II / event\}. F1${=}0.00$: correct span, wrong type, plus hallucinated entity.

\item \textbf{Type confusion (minimal).} \textit{``...the deployment of the `SPQ' template...''} Gold: \{SPQ / organization\}. All 8 samples: \{SPQ / \textbf{product}\}. F1${=}0.00$: entity text matches exactly but type disagrees across all samples.

\item \textbf{Complete miss.} \textit{``On stage, the band uses different kinds of instruments like synths, guitars, cello, glockenspiel and a bass played with a sickle.''} Gold: 6 entities (synths, guitars, cello, glockenspiel, bass, sickle / product). All 8 samples: $\emptyset$. F1${=}0.00$: total recall failure on all gold entities.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{LP confidence failures (3/3).}
High log-probability does not guarantee correctness at the entity level. These entities appear in all 8 samples with near-zero negative log-probability (high confidence), yet are absent from the gold annotation.

\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item \textit{``Cramer pitched for the Orange County Flyers of the independent Golden League in 2008.''} Entity: Cramer / person (mean LP${=}{-}0.046$, 8/8 samples). Gold: \{Orange County Flyers / org, independent Golden League / org\}. Plausible entity, not annotated.

\item \textit{``...according to UK Royal Air Force Wing Commander and FOD researcher Richard Friend.''} Entity: Richard Friend / person (mean LP${=}{-}0.050$, 8/8). Gold: \{UK Royal Air Force / org, FOD / org\}. Likely annotation gap: Richard Friend is a real person mentioned by name; gold omits it.

\item \textit{``...the Navy's forces within South Vietnam were operationally controlled by COMUSMACV.''} Entity: COMUSMACV / org (mean LP${=}{-}0.050$, 8/8). Gold: \{Seventh Fleet / org, South Vietnam / location\}. Model confidently extracts a valid entity missing from gold.
\end{itemize}

\noindent These examples highlight a fundamental limitation: LP signals the model's confidence, not correctness. When the model is correctly confident about entities that gold annotations omit, LP cannot serve as an error detector.

\paragraph{Consensus-based verification failures (3/3).}
Entity consensus frequency (fraction of $N$ samples containing a given entity) serves as the primary self-verification signal. It fails in both directions.

\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item \textbf{Overconfident.} \textit{``Les Blank...was an American documentary filmmaker best known for his portraits of American traditional musicians.''} Entity: American / location (8/8 samples, consensus${=}1.0$). Gold: \{Les Blank / person\}. Maximum consensus for non-gold entity.

\item \textbf{Overconfident.} \textit{``Cramer pitched for the Orange County Flyers of the independent Golden League in 2008.''} Entity: Cramer / person (8/8 samples, consensus${=}1.0$). Gold: \{Orange County Flyers / org, independent Golden League / org\}. Same instance as LP failure above---simultaneous failure of both signals.

\item \textbf{Underconfident.} \textit{``They finished the season 14--19, 9--9 in C-USA play to finish in seventh place.''} Gold entity: C-USA play / event (consensus${=}0.0$, never predicted in any of 8 samples). Zero consensus for a correct entity.
\end{itemize}

\noindent These examples illustrate that the failure modes identified by the diagnostic cascade are not statistical abstractions but manifest in individual instances. The LP and consensus failures frequently co-occur (e.g., ``Cramer'' instance), confirming that the signals share common blind spots rather than providing independent error detection.

5	\paragraph{Datasets.}
6	We evaluate on four English NER benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient.
7	\textbf{SciERC} \cite{luan2018scierc} (551 test instances, 6 entity types) is the primary medium-difficulty test bed (${\approx}$65\% F1).
8	\textbf{Few-NERD} \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (INTRA coarse; 37{,}648 instances, 8 entity types, ${\approx}$75\% F1) provides a low-degeneracy contrast where LP selection succeeds (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}).
9	\textbf{CoNLL-2003} \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (3{,}453 test sentences, 4 entity types, ${\approx}$91\% F1) serves as a ceiling-effect control.
10	\textbf{WNUT-17} \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (1{,}287 social media instances, 51\% zero F1) probes the signal-collapse boundary.

12	\paragraph{Models and sampling.}

24	\noindent\textbf{Degeneracy Decomposition.}\label{thm:degeneracy_bound}
25	For any aggregation method $A$: $\mathbb{E}[\Delta F_1(A)] \leq (1 - D) \cdot G_{\textup{nd}}$,
26	where $D$ is the degeneracy rate and $G_{\textup{nd}}$ the oracle gap on non-degenerate instances.
27	For signal-based methods with alignment $\alpha \in [0,1]$, this tightens to $(1{-}D) \cdot G_{\textup{nd}} \cdot \alpha$ (proof in Appendix~\ref{app:bound_proof}).
28	
29	\noindent With $G_{\textup{nd}}{\approx}14.8$\,pp and $\alpha{\approx}0.068$, the critical threshold is $\theta_{\textup{crit}}{=}0.70$ (a data-dependent empirical approximation): when $D{>}70$\%, SC gain falls below $0.3$\,pp.
30	Across 16 configurations, all gains respect the bound (ratio 3--12\%; empirical validation: Figure~\ref{fig:bound}); the bound is loose because $\alpha$---not $D$---is the bottleneck.
31	Tightening requires improving within-instance alignment, which neither signal combination (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}) nor verifier-based construction (\S\ref{sec:verifier}) achieves.

\paragraph{MV neutrality under aggregate micro-F1.}
Computing entity-level micro-F1 (aggregate TP/FP/FN across all instances) confirms MV${\approx}$greedy: Few-NERD $\Delta{=}{-}0.83{\pm}0.38$\,pp, CoNLL $+0.16{\pm}0.17$\,pp, SciERC $+0.15{\pm}0.18$\,pp (multi-seed; Appendix~\ref{app:alpha_crit}).
Defining $\alpha_{\textup{crit}} = \pi_{\textup{MV}} / (2 - \pi_{\textup{MV}})$ as the per-sample accuracy threshold required for MV to outperform greedy, CoNLL yields $\alpha_{\textup{crit,eff}} = \alpha_{\textup{crit}} / (1{-}\delta) > 1.0$, meaning MV gain is \textit{structurally impossible} given 60\% degeneracy.
The conclusion holds under both macro- and micro-F1; the near-zero $|\Delta|$ is not an artifact of metric choice.

1052	\begin{definition}[Instance-Level Degeneracy]
1053	Given model $\mathcal{M}$, input $x$, and $N$ i.i.d.\ samples $\{y_1, \ldots, y_N\}$, instance $x$ is \emph{degenerate} if $y_1 = \cdots = y_N$. The degeneracy rate is $D = |\mathcal{D}|^{-1} \sum_{x} \mathbb{1}[y_1(x) = \cdots = y_N(x)]$.
1054	\end{definition}
1055	
1056	\begin{definition}[Non-Degenerate Oracle Gap]
1057	$G_{\text{nd}} = \mathbb{E}[F_1^{\text{oracle}}(x) - F_1^{\text{greedy}}(x) \mid x \in \mathcal{D}_{\neg D}]$, where $\mathcal{D}_{\neg D}$ is the set of non-degenerate instances.
1058	\end{definition}

1061	
1062	Partition $\mathcal{D}$ into degenerate ($\mathcal{D}_D$, fraction $D$) and non-degenerate ($\mathcal{D}_{\neg D}$, fraction $1{-}D$). By total expectation:

1064	\mathbb{E}[\Delta F_1(A)] = D \cdot \mathbb{E}[\Delta F_1 \mid \mathcal{D}_D] + (1{-}D) \cdot \mathbb{E}[\Delta F_1 \mid \mathcal{D}_{\neg D}].
1065	\end{equation}
1066	For degenerate instances, all $N$ samples are identical and equal the greedy output, so $\Delta F_1 = 0$.
